entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Virginia Woolf (1882–1941) was an English writer and modernist pioneer whose novels—including 'Mrs Dalloway' (1925), 'To the Lighthouse' (1927), and 'Orlando' (1928)—revolutionised narrative technique through stream-of-consciousness prose that mapped the interior landscape of human thought with unprecedented precision.

Born into the intellectual aristocracy of Victorian London (her father was Sir Leslie Stephen, editor of the Dictionary of National Biography), Woolf suffered from recurring mental illness throughout her life. She and her husband Leonard founded the Hogarth Press in 1917, which published T.S. Eliot's 'The Waste Land' and her own experimental novels.

Her essay 'A Room of One's Own' (1929) argued that women's literary achievement required financial independence and private space—a foundational text of feminist literary criticism. 'Three Guineas' (1938) connected patriarchy, fascism, and war in a prescient analysis that anticipated second-wave feminism by decades.

Woolf was central to the Bloomsbury Group—the London intellectual circle that included John Maynard Keynes, E.M. Forster, and Lytton Strachey. She drowned herself in the River Ouse on March 28, 1941, leaving a note to Leonard: 'I don't think two people could have been happier than we have been.'

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Virginia Woolf's innovative stream-of-consciousness prose in novels like 'Mrs Dalloway' and 'To the Lighthouse' influenced generations of writers, shaping modernist literature and feminist thought. Her advocacy for women's financial independence through her essay 'A Room of One's Own' continues to inspire literary scholars and activists.
